hints: For each quantity, identify energy and charge.
Keep the source role separate from the component role.
walkthrough: Recall that both quantities compare an energy transfer with charge.
For e.m.f., identify energy supplied or transferred by the source per unit charge.
For potential difference, identify energy transferred or work done per unit charge across the component.
State the two roles separately.

ai_rubric.observable: Defines e.m.f. as energy supplied or transferred by a source per unit charge
Defines potential difference as energy transferred or work done per unit charge

evidence.evidence_gap: Original diagnostic options isolate energy-transfer and charge-used-up misconceptions.

hints: Ask what happens to energy per coulomb inside a real cell.
walkthrough: The e.m.f. gives the total energy supplied per coulomb.
A current through internal resistance transfers some electrical energy to thermal energy inside the cell.
The terminal p.d. is the smaller energy per coulomb available outside.
Therefore option C is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects C: terminal p.d. is less than e.m.f. because energy per unit charge is transferred inside the cell

evidence.evidence_gap: Values and cell context are original.

hints: Calculate Ir before subtracting it from the e.m.f.
walkthrough: Known values are 𝓔 = 4.5 V, I = 0.50 A and r = 0.60 Ω.
Lost volts are Ir = 0.50 × 0.60 = 0.30 V.
Terminal p.d. is V = 4.5 - 0.30 = 4.2 V.
Therefore option C is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects C by calculating V = 4.5 - (0.50 × 0.60) = 4.2 V

hints: Keep 𝓔 and r fixed and focus on the product Ir.
walkthrough: Increasing the external resistance lowers current in this stated simple-load situation.
With fixed r, lower current makes Ir smaller.
In V = 𝓔 - Ir, a smaller amount is subtracted from unchanged 𝓔.
Terminal p.d. increases, so option D is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects D: lower current makes Ir smaller, so V = 𝓔 - Ir increases

evidence.evidence_gap: Weather-station context and values are original.

hints: Find Ir first, then carry it into V = 𝓔 - Ir.
walkthrough: The current through the internal resistance is 0.75 A.
Calculate Ir = 0.75 × 0.40 = 0.30 V.
Subtract this from the source e.m.f.: V = 7.2 - 0.30 = 6.9 V.
The 0.30 V represents 0.30 J transferred inside the source for each coulomb, so less energy per coulomb remains outside.

hints: Lost volts equal current multiplied by internal resistance.
walkthrough: Known values are I = 0.75 A and r = 0.40 Ω.
Use lost volts = Ir.
Report 0.30 V to two significant figures.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses lost volts = Ir with I = 0.75 A and r = 0.40 Ω
Obtains 0.30 V

hints: Subtract the internal loss from the e.m.f.
walkthrough: Carry forward the internal loss 0.30 V.
Use V = 𝓔 - Ir.
Substitute: V = 7.2 - 0.30 = 6.90 V.
Report 6.9 V to two significant figures.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses V = 𝓔 - Ir or subtracts the 0.30 V internal loss from 7.2 V
Obtains 6.9 V

hints: Describe what happens to energy per coulomb inside the source.
walkthrough: The e.m.f. is the total source energy supplied per coulomb.
Current through internal resistance transfers some of this energy to thermal energy inside the source.
The external circuit therefore receives less energy per coulomb, so terminal p.d. is below e.m.f.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that energy per unit charge is transferred inside the source, leaving terminal p.d. below e.m.f.

evidence.evidence_gap: Inspection-lamp context, circuit and values are original.

hints: The difference between e.m.f. and terminal p.d. is Ir.
walkthrough: Read 𝓔 = 9.6 V, V = 8.4 V and I = 1.20 A from the simple circuit.
Find the internal loss: 9.6 - 8.4 = 1.2 V.
Then Pinternal = I²r = 1.20² × 1.0 = 1.44 W, or 1.4 W to two significant figures.

hints: Find 𝓔 - V before dividing by current.
walkthrough: Known values are 𝓔 = 9.6 V, V = 8.4 V and I = 1.20 A.
The internal voltage loss is 𝓔 - V = 1.2 V.
Since 𝓔 - V = Ir, rearrange to r = (𝓔 - V)/I.
Substitute r = 1.2/1.20 = 1.0 Ω.

ai_rubric.observable: Finds the internal voltage loss as 9.6 - 8.4 = 1.2 V
Uses r = (𝓔 - V)/I with I = 1.20 A
Obtains 1.0 Ω

hints: Use the current and internal resistance, or the current and internal voltage loss.
walkthrough: Carry forward I = 1.20 A and r = 1.0 Ω.
Use Pinternal = I²r.
Substitute: Pinternal = 1.20² × 1.0 = 1.44 W.
Report 1.4 W to two significant figures. As a check, I(𝓔 - V) = 1.20 × 1.2 gives the same 1.44 W.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses Pinternal = I²r or I(𝓔 - V) with consistent values
Obtains 1.44 W, or 1.4 W to two significant figures

evidence.evidence_gap: Tracking-beacon context, two operating modes, values and diagram are original.

hints: Keep the same e.m.f. and r in both modes.
For source power use the energy supplied per coulomb multiplied by coulombs per second.
walkthrough: First use Lesson 2: e.m.f. is total source energy supplied per coulomb, while terminal p.d. is the energy per coulomb available externally.
In normal mode, Ir = 0.50 × 0.80 = 0.40 V, so V = 11.6 V.
In burst mode, Ir = 2.0 × 0.80 = 1.6 V, so V = 10.4 V.
Source power is 𝓔I: 6.0 W normally and 24 W in burst mode.
The higher-current burst mode has more source power but a lower terminal p.d. because its internal loss per coulomb is larger.

hints: Compare total source energy per coulomb with the part available outside.
walkthrough: The 12.0 V e.m.f. means the battery supplies 12.0 J to each coulomb.
As current passes through internal resistance, some energy per coulomb is transferred to thermal energy inside the battery.
The remaining energy per coulomb is transferred externally, so the terminal p.d. is below 12.0 V.

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies e.m.f. as the total energy supplied by the battery per unit charge
Explains that some energy per unit charge is transferred in the internal resistance, leaving a lower terminal p.d.

hints: Use the normal-mode current in V = 𝓔 - Ir.
walkthrough: Normal mode has I = 0.50 A.
Lost volts are Ir = 0.50 × 0.80 = 0.40 V.
Report 11.6 V to three significant figures.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses V = 𝓔 - Ir with I = 0.50 A and r = 0.80 Ω
Obtains 11.6 V

hints: Use the burst-mode current and keep e.m.f. and r unchanged.
walkthrough: Burst mode has I = 2.0 A.
Lost volts are Ir = 2.0 × 0.80 = 1.60 V.
Report 10.4 V to three significant figures. It is lower than 11.6 V as expected for the larger current.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses V = 𝓔 - Ir with I = 2.0 A and r = 0.80 Ω
Obtains 10.4 V

hints: Source power uses e.m.f., not terminal p.d.: Psource = 𝓔I.
walkthrough: The source supplies 12.0 J per coulomb in both modes.
Normal mode power is P = 12.0 × 0.50 = 6.0 W.
Burst mode power is P = 12.0 × 2.0 = 24 W.
Because 24 W is greater than 6.0 W, burst mode has the greater source power.
This is consistent with fixed e.m.f. and a fourfold current increase.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses source power P = 𝓔I to obtain 6.0 W in normal mode and 24 W in burst mode
States that burst mode has the greater source power

audit.originality: All learner contexts, wording, numerical values and planned figures are original and do not reproduce mapped official questions.
audit.scope: All required solutions use one source with internal resistance and one simple external load. No junction, multi-loop, general Kirchhoff, combined-resistance or potential-divider method is required.
audit.evidence: All four canonical Lesson 3 P2 evidence leaves were inspected together with their whole-question contexts; P1 evidence remains deferred and was not inferred.
audit.numerical_recomputation: Every product, difference, internal resistance, terminal p.d., source power, internal power, unit, tolerance and significant-figure statement was independently recomputed.
audit.learner_answer_separation: Questions contain prompts and response schemas only. Answers, marking criteria, feedback and walkthroughs remain answer-side.
